blocks.text: The prompt completion format is the simplest structure a fine-tuning dataset can take, each example is just a prompt and the completion that should follow it, with no roles, no turns, and no extra metadata beyond those two fields.

It predates the more elaborate chat message format covered earlier in this module, and while many modern fine-tuning workflows have moved toward chat style data, prompt completion format still fits certain tasks well and remains worth understanding on its own terms.
1. The Simplest Fine-Tuning Format
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359756-264171427.png
In this format, a training example is nothing more than a prompt string and a completion string, the completion being exactly what the model should learn to generate when given that prompt.
There is no role labeling, no system message, no conversation history, just the plainest possible input to output pairing.
2. Prompt and Completion, Defined

The prompt is everything the model sees before it starts generating, and the completion is everything the model is expected to generate in response, together forming one continuous sequence once combined for training.
3. When This Format Fits Best
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359756-725348196.png

Prompt completion format works cleanly for tasks that are genuinely single turn and self contained, translation, classification, straightforward text transformation, where there is no back and forth exchange to represent.
It becomes awkward for anything involving multiple turns or distinct roles, since it has no built in way to represent a conversation history or distinguish a system instruction from a user message.
4. The Boundary Between Prompt and Completion

blocks.alt: The Boundary Between Prompt and Completion
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359952-290249072.png

When a prompt completion example gets combined into one sequence for actual training, there needs to be a clear, consistent way to mark where the prompt ends and the completion begins, whether through a fixed separator string or a special token, so the model, and the training code, can reliably tell the two apart.
5. Prompt Completion vs Chat Message Format

blocks.alt: Prompt Completion vs Chat Message Format
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359953-955834750.png

Chat message format, covered in the Chat Templates topic earlier in this module, generalizes this same basic idea, prompt in, response out, across multiple roles and multiple turns, using a model specific template to handle the structure.

blocks.text: 6. Loss Masking, Training Only on the Completion

blocks.alt: Loss Masking, Training Only on the Completion
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359953-503518849.png

Even though the prompt and completion are combined into one sequence for training, the loss, the signal the model actually learns from, is typically computed only over the completion portion, not the prompt.

This matters because the prompt is context the model is given, not something it needs to learn to generate, training on it as if it were the target would waste training signal and can subtly distort what the model actually learns to prioritize.

blocks.title: This same idea reappears in the Tokenization Pipeline topic
blocks.content: Masking loss so it only applies to the portion the model should learn to generate, rather than the input context, is a pattern that carries over directly into chat format fine-tuning as well.

blocks.text: 7. Limitations of This Format
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359954-416216626.png

Beyond its inability to represent multi-turn conversation naturally, prompt completion format also has no clean way to express a persistent system level instruction that should apply across many different prompts, something chat format handles directly through its dedicated system role.
8. A Practical Use Case Where This Format Still Shines

For narrow, well defined tasks, a classifier that always takes one input and produces one label, a text normalizer that always takes messy input and produces cleaned output, the simplicity of prompt completion format is a genuine advantage, with less structural overhead than chat format requires.
9. Migrating From Prompt Completion to Chat Format

blocks.alt: Migrating From Prompt Completion to Chat Format
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359954-297103006.png

If a task that started out single turn eventually needs to support conversation or a persistent system instruction, an existing prompt completion dataset can usually be migrated fairly directly, the prompt becomes a user turn, the completion becomes an assistant turn, with a system message added as needed.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a model purely to convert informal notes into formal meeting minutes uses prompt completion format, since the task is genuinely single turn, one note in, one formal version out, with no conversational back and forth involved at all.

Choosing this simpler format over chat format keeps their dataset preparation pipeline lighter, with no need to design system prompts, roles, or multi-turn structure for a task that never actually needs any of that.
Common Mistakes

items: Forcing a genuinely multi-turn task into prompt completion format, losing conversational context
Computing training loss over the full sequence, including the prompt, instead of masking it to the completion only
Using an inconsistent or ambiguous boundary marker between the prompt and completion across examples
Sticking with prompt completion format after a task has grown to genuinely need multi-turn or system level structure

blocks.text: Practice

Take a task you are considering fine-tuning for, and decide honestly whether it is truly single turn, prompt completion format fits well, or whether it secretly needs conversational structure, in which case chat format is the better starting point.
Key Takeaway

Prompt completion format pairs a plain prompt with a plain completion, the simplest possible fine-tuning shape, well suited to genuinely single turn tasks but limited once a task needs multiple turns or a persistent system instruction, at which point migrating to chat message format is the natural next step.
